answers.question: Is the small-signal model of a PMOS device identical to that of an NMOS device?

The small-signal (hybrid-\(\pi\)) equivalent circuit of a MOSFET is obtained by linearizing the large-signal \(I\)-\(V\) characteristics about a DC bias point. Because the linearization is performed on incremental voltages and currents, the resulting controlled sources (\(g_m v_{gs}\), \(g_{mb} v_{bs}\)) and the small-signal resistances and capacitances have identical topologies and polarities for both device types. Consequently the same equivalent circuit is used for NMOS and PMOS transistors (only the numerical values of the parameters differ).

Final answer: yes

The LDO output voltage \(V_\text{out}\) sets the DC common-mode level at the tank nodes \(X,Y\). Consequently the varactors (and other voltage-dependent capacitances) experience a bias of \(V_\text{out}-V_\text{cont}\), producing a supply-pushing sensitivity
\[
K_{VDD}=\frac{\partial f_\text{osc}}{\partial V_\text{out}}\qquad(\text{Hz/V}).
\]
A voltage-noise spectrum \(S_\text{th}\) (one-sided, \(\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}\)) therefore appears as a frequency-noise spectrum \(K_{VDD}^2S_\text{th}\). Converting frequency noise to phase and taking the single-sideband definition of phase noise yields
\[
\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=\frac{K_{VDD}^2S_\text{th}}{2(\Delta f)^2}.
\]

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=K_{VDD}^2 S_{th}/[2(\Delta f)^2]\)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies supply pushing, converts the LDO noise to frequency noise, and gives the 1/Δf² phase-noise dependence. It notes the direct varactor biasing but does not state that Kpush is closely related to KVCO or that reducing KVCO reduces the conversion.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
The LDO output \(V_\text{out}\) is the VCO supply (DC voltage at the tank nodes \(X,Y\)). Consequently the oscillation frequency depends on \(V_\text{out}\) through the varactor bias (\(V_\text{out}-V_\text{cont}\)) and through supply pushing of the cross-coupled pair; the resulting sensitivity is the pushing factor
\[
K_{VDD}=\frac{\partial f_\text{osc}}{\partial V_\text{out}}\qquad(\text{Hz/V}).
\]
A voltage fluctuation \(v_n(t)\) on \(V_\text{out}\) therefore produces an instantaneous frequency deviation \(K_{VDD}v_n(t)\). The corresponding excess phase is the integral of that deviation, which in the frequency domain multiplies the (one-sided) noise spectrum \(S_\text{th}\) by \((K_{VDD}/f_m)^2\). Converting to single-sideband phase noise yields
\[
\mathcal{L}(f_m)=\frac{K_{VDD}^2}{2f_m^2}S_\text{th}.
\]

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(f_m)=K_{VDD}^2 S_{th}/(2f_m^2)\)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies supply pushing, uses the frequency sensitivity, and applies FM-to-phase conversion with the expected 1/f_m^2 dependence. It omits the design insight that Kpush is closely related to KVCO here, so reducing KVCO reduces this noise conversion.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
The LDO output noise appears as a voltage disturbance on the oscillator supply node \(V_\text{out}\). This modulates the instantaneous oscillation frequency through the VCO supply-pushing factor
\[
K_\text{push}=\frac{\partial f_\text{osc}}{\partial V_\text{out}}
\]
(principally via the voltage dependence of the MOS varactors and of the parasitic capacitances of \(M_1,M_2\)).

A sinusoidal supply disturbance of peak amplitude \(A\) therefore produces a peak frequency deviation \(K_\text{push}A\). The resulting modulation index at offset \(f_m\) is \(\beta=K_\text{push}A/f_m\), and each PM sideband relative to the carrier is \((\beta/2)^2\). Replacing the sine-wave by a one-sided noise density \(S_\text{th}\) (so that \(A=\sqrt{2S_\text{th}}\) in a 1 Hz bandwidth) immediately yields the single-sideband phase noise
\[
\mathcal{L}(f_m)=10\log_{10}\Bigl(\frac{K_\text{push}^2S_\text{th}}{2f_m^2}\Bigr).
\]

(The same result follows from the frequency-modulation relation \(S_\phi(f)=(K_\text{push}/f)^2S_\text{th}\) together with the definition \(\mathcal{L}=S_\phi/2\).) Direct additive leakage of the LDO noise onto the differential outputs \(X-Y\) is rejected by symmetry and does not contribute to \(\mathcal{L}\).

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(f_m)=10\log_{10}(K_\text{push}^2 S_\text{th}/(2f_m^2))\)

answer.text:
The circuit is a standard cross-coupled LC oscillator. Noise from the tail current source around \(2\omega_0\) is mixed to the oscillation frequency by the switching action of \(M_1/M_2\) and appears as phase noise. The added capacitor \(C_T\) shunts this noise away from the differential pair, reducing the phase-noise contribution of \(I_{SS}\).

Final answer: phase noise decreases

answer.text:
The circuit is a standard NMOS cross-coupled LC oscillator. Thermal noise from \(I_{SS}\) near \(2\omega_0\) is mixed down to the carrier by the switching action of \(M_1/M_2\) and appears as phase noise. The added capacitor \(C_T\) shunts this noise to ground, suppressing the mixing process (it also reduces the associated AM-to-PM conversion). Consequently the phase-noise contribution of the tail source falls and overall oscillator phase noise improves.

Final answer: PN decreases (tail noise filtered)

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit consists of two identical differential LC oscillators that are coupled (via the additional differential pairs biased at \(I_1\)) so as to run in quadrature. Each oscillator employs a pair of inductors as the tank inductance. Although explicit tank capacitors are not drawn, they are invariably present (either as added capacitors/varactors or as the parasitics of the transistors and inductors). Consequently the free-running frequency of each tank, and therefore the oscillation frequency of the coupled system, is the tank resonance

\[
f_\text{osc}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}.
\]

(The coupling produced by \(I_1\) introduces only a small fractional shift of order \(I_1/I_\text{SS}Q\), which is neglected in a first-order estimate.)

Final answer: \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\)

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit consists of two identical differential LC oscillators with parallel coupling (via the additional transistor pairs biased by \(I_1\)) to enforce a quadrature relationship between the two tanks. Each tank therefore oscillates at (or extremely near) its natural resonant frequency

\[
f_\text{osc}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}},
\]

where \(L\) is the inductance shown in the schematic and \(C\) is the total capacitance appearing in parallel with that inductance (explicit tank capacitors plus device parasitics). The coupling currents produce only a small shift away from this value, of second order in the coupling factor \(I_1/I_\text{SS}\).

Final answer: \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the uncoupled tank resonance, but omits the first-order coupling-induced frequency shift and incorrectly describes that shift as second order in the coupling factor.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit consists of two identical LC oscillators. Each oscillator is formed from a differential LC tank together with a cross-coupled NMOS pair (biased by \(I_{SS}\)) that supplies the negative resistance needed to sustain oscillation. (The tank capacitors are omitted from the schematic but are understood to lie in parallel with the drawn inductors.)

The remaining NMOS pairs (biased by \(I_1\)) have their gates driven by the opposite oscillator, thereby coupling the two tanks. The sense of the coupling forces the two oscillators into quadrature lock, producing the four phases \(X_1,Y_1,X_2,Y_2\).

Because the coupling transistors appear in parallel with the regenerative pairs, they contribute only a small reactive current. Consequently the oscillation frequency remains essentially the tank resonance:
\[
f_\text{osc}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}.
\]

Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\)
